nameStory: The Virginia ctenucha gets its name from the state where it was first scientifically described back in 1794. The unusual word 'ctenucha' comes from a Greek term meaning 'small comb,' likely referring to the feathery, comb-like antennae that males of this species sport.
description: The Virginia ctenucha is a striking day-flying moth that many people mistake for a butterfly at first glance. Adults have metallic blue-black wings with a wingspan of about 1.5-2 inches, and their bodies are covered in iridescent blue-black scales that shimmer in sunlight. Unlike most moths, they're active during the day and fly with a slow, deliberate pattern rather than the erratic flight of typical moths. Their caterpillars are fuzzy yellow and black creatures that feed on grasses and sedges.

idTips.label: Metallic blue-black wings
idTips.description: Wings appear deep metallic blue-black with an oily sheen that shifts colors in different light angles, feeling smooth and velvety if gently touched

idTips.label: Day-flying behavior
idTips.description: Active during sunny daylight hours with slow, steady flight pattern unlike most moths; often seen nectaring on flowers during mid-morning to afternoon

idTips.label: Orange head patch
idTips.description: Bright orange-red fuzzy patch on the head that contrasts sharply with the dark body, visible when viewed head-on

idTips.label: Feathery antennae
idTips.description: Males have distinctly feathery, comb-like antennae that feel delicate and branched, while females have thinner, thread-like antennae

idTips.label: Iridescent body
idTips.description: Body covered in metallic blue-green scales that feel smooth and create a rainbow sheen when the light hits just right

habitat: Virginia ctenucha moths prefer open grasslands, meadows, and marsh edges throughout New England, especially areas with native grasses and sedges where their caterpillars feed. You'll often spot them in coastal salt marshes, wet meadows, and prairie-like openings in forests. They're particularly fond of areas with goldenrod, asters, and other late-season wildflowers that provide nectar for the adults.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active yet; overwintered pupae are developing underground. Caterpillars from the previous year may still be visible as fuzzy yellow and black larvae feeding on new grass growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time from mid-July through August when adults are most visible nectaring on flowers during warm, sunny days. This is the best time to observe their distinctive day-flying behavior and metallic wings.
seasonality.fall: Flight period continues into early September, with mating and egg-laying occurring. Late-season flowers like goldenrod and asters attract the remaining adults before they die off.
seasonality.winter: No visible activity; pupae rest underground in the soil, waiting for spring warmth to trigger their final transformation to adults.

funFact: Despite being a moth, Virginia ctenucha adults are terrible at coming to lights at night because they're actually programmed to sleep when it gets dark—they're one of the few moths that have completely switched to a daytime lifestyle, essentially becoming honorary butterflies!
confusionNotes: Often mistaken for a dark butterfly due to its day-flying habits and metallic wings, but butterflies hold their wings vertically when at rest while ctenucha moths rest with wings horizontal like a tiny airplane. The orange head patch and feathery antennae (in males) are dead giveaways that you're looking at a moth, not a butterfly.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name can be tricky to pronounce—it's "ten-OO-ka"—and many field guides place this species in different moth families depending on their publication date, as moth classification has been recently reorganized based on DNA studies. Don't be confused if you see it listed under different family names in older books.
compareHints: Virginia ctenucha is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it relatively easy to identify among the ctenucha moths. Within the broader erebid moth family, it's most similar to other metallic day-flying species like the eight-spotted forester, but that species has distinct white spots on black wings rather than the solid metallic blue-black of the Virginia ctenucha. The combination of orange head patch and uniform dark wings makes it distinctive among New England's day-flying moths.
